formationLabel: St. Lawrence Society formed in 1902 · Lithuanian mission met in rented halls by about 1907 · St. Ambrose chapel cornerstone blessed July 11, 1909 · final Mass Christmas 1964 · property liquidation voted in 1965
currentUse: The St. Ambrose mission chapel was demolished after the mission's final Mass at Christmas 1964 and the remaining members' 1965 vote to liquidate the property. A near-period source summarized by Wolkovich says a small apartment complex replaced the chapel within months. The exact former address, parcel, present apartment identity, and current use as of 2026 remain unresolved.
summary: St. Ambrose was a Lithuanian Roman Catholic mission at Port Washington, not an independently proven parish. A St. Lawrence Society formed in 1902, the community met in rented halls by about 1907, and the St. Ambrose chapel cornerstone was blessed July 11, 1909. The mission was pastorally dependent on Immaculate Conception in Sheboygan; by 1921 the Sheboygan pastor offered Mass twice monthly. The final Mass occurred at Christmas 1964. In 1965 the twelve remaining members voted to liquidate the property, after which the chapel was demolished and replaced by a small apartment complex. The dossier preserves 1964 as the last-worship date and 1965 as the liquidation/building-disposition phase, rather than forcing one closure year. No later parish erection, successor, records custodian, cemetery, or exact street address has been verified.

historicalNarrative.text: St. Ambrose began as a mission community rather than a proven parish. Lithuanian workers in Port Washington formed the St. Lawrence Society in 1902 and, within several years, met in rented halls. This organizational stage is separate from the chapel and from any canonical parish erection; no source reviewed for this dossier shows that the Archdiocese later elevated the mission to parish status.

historicalNarrative.text: The cornerstone for the 100-seat St. Ambrose chapel was blessed July 11, 1909. Wolkovich describes about thirty Lithuanian families and fifty single adults supporting the mission. By 1921 the pastor of Immaculate Conception in Sheboygan offered Mass at St. Ambrose twice each month, documenting a mission-of relationship without merging the two institutional identities.

sources.locator: Wolkovich, vol. 3, PDF p. 38 / printed p. 30; chapel, membership, and twice-monthly service from Sheboygan

historicalNarrative.text: The Sheboygan parish history elsewhere in Wolkovich also counted roughly fifty St. Ambrose mission families in 1916. This reinforces the dependent pastoral structure while showing a functioning local community with its own chapel. The dossier does not convert this size or longevity into evidence of an independent juridic parish.

historicalNarrative.text: St. Ambrose's terminal sequence spans two calendar years. Wolkovich, citing the Catholic Herald Citizen and Port Pilot, says the final Mass took place at Christmas 1964. By 1965 only twelve members remained and voted to liquidate the property. The case therefore records 1964 as the end of documented worship and 1965 as the institutional/property disposition phase, leaving the canonical suppression date unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: The chapel was demolished and a small apartment complex replaced it within months, according to the near-period account summarized by Wolkovich. That evidence establishes demolition and historical replacement, not the exact parcel address or the apartments' current identity in 2026. The Archdiocese's current closed/merged-parish page does not list St. Ambrose, so no successor, sacramental-record custodian, cemetery, or canonical instrument is inferred from omission.
